title: Pink or Reddish Lettuce: What It Means and Whether You Can Eat It

seo.title: Pink or Reddish Lettuce: Is It Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: Pink or red ribs are often a physiological storage disorder or tissue-injury response. If lettuce is still firm with no mold, slime, or foul odor, color alone does not mean spoilage.
seo.search_intent: Understand why lettuce turns pink or reddish and distinguish cosmetic discoloration from true spoilage.

excerpt: Pink or reddish ribs do not automatically mean lettuce is bad. UC Davis describes pink rib as a postharvest physiological disorder associated with overmaturity, long storage, or warmer-than-recommended conditions. If leaves remain reasonably crisp with no mold, slime, or off odor, the discoloration is usually a quality issue.
content_html:
Lettuce can develop pink, red, or brown streaks along the ribs even when the leaves are not rotten. Color alone is not proof of spoilage. Several physiological disorders and injury responses create pigments without necessarily involving microbial decay.

What “pink rib” is

UC Davis describes pink rib as a postharvest disorder in which leaf veins and the base develop pinkish or reddish color. It is more common in overmature heads, lettuce stored too long, or lettuce held above recommended temperatures.

Cuts and broken ribs can also trigger phenolic reactions that turn damaged tissue pink or brown.

When it is still usable

If the lettuce is reasonably crisp, smells normal, and has no mold, slimy film, or rotten watery tissue, limited discoloration is mainly a quality issue. You can trim unattractive parts if you prefer.

When to discard it

  • Slime or a sticky coating.
  • Sour, fermented, or rotten odor.
  • Visible mold.
  • Watery tissue that breaks down easily.
  • Widespread discoloration combined with overall decay.

How to slow the change

Keep lettuce cold, avoid crushing it, and limit free moisture. Low temperature slows respiration, yellowing, discoloration, and decay.

Pink by itself is usually a quality signal; pink plus slime, mold, or rot is a different decision.

faq.question: Is pink lettuce spoiled?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Pink rib is a recognized physiological storage disorder and can occur without decay.

faq.question: Can I trim the reddish part and eat the rest?
faq.answer: Yes if the remaining lettuce is crisp, smells normal, and shows no mold, slime, or rot.

faq.question: Why does it happen near the end of storage life?
faq.answer: Long storage, overmaturity, warmer temperatures, and mechanical injury all favor discoloration.
